note: Findings against existing provisions, filed as draft amendments rather than applied. Under Axiom A3 the only route from a case — or from a corpus author — to a rule change is a draft amendment the legislative process may adopt or reject.

amendments.finding: The provision cites only 'California SB 53 (15-day / 24-hour)'. Verified: EU AI Act Art. 55(1)(c) has bound systemic-risk GPAI providers since 2 Aug 2025 to report serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and it attaches at the 10^25 FLOP presumption, not SB 53's 10^26 — so a run can owe an EU report and no Californian one. Separately, SB 53 is under the EO 14365 preemption challenge and the pack carries no instability flag on it.
amendments.proposed: Restate the citation as 'California SB 53 §22757.13 (15-day / 24-hour; under EO 14365 preemption challenge); EU AI Act Art. 55(1)(c); GPAI Code of Practice Commitment 9'. Leave the provision ordinary; the extension's FL-TR-004 carries the configurability floor for the clock itself, and the two should be read together.
amendments.why_not_applied: Changing a provision's stated source changes what a later adjudicator reasons from. That is a legislative act under A3, not an editorial one.

amendments.finding: Both weight-security absolutes rest on 'California SB 53' plus RAND security levels (FL-SF-002) and on 'practice policy; RAND SL3+ paraphrased' (FL-SF-003). The strongest binding source — EU AI Act Art. 55(1)(d), in force since 2 Aug 2025, with GPAI Code of Practice Commitment 6 / Measure 6.2 / Appendix 4 as the presumption-of-conformity route — is cited by neither. FL-SF-003 is an absolute whose only external authority is a noncommercial-use-only report; as written it reads as a severity claim rather than a who-may-decide floor.
amendments.proposed: Add Art. 55(1)(d) and Code of Practice Commitment 6 to both citations. Keep both absolute: the two-person rule is the access-control floor that Measure 6.2 names, and the citation change gives it the statutory footing its absolute status needs.
amendments.why_not_applied: The 290 F-absolute cases in the shipped corpus cite these provisions as they stand; re-grounding a floor is for the responsible-scaling council, not the corpus author.

amendments.finding: The provision cites 'EU AI Act Art. 14(4)–(5)' alongside GDPR Art. 22(3) and the CPPA ADMT regulations as if all three bound now. Verified: Art. 14 sits in the Annex III high-risk block that Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 deferred to 2 Dec 2027 — the same deferral the pack itself records on FL-GV-009, FL-GV-010 and FL-GV-011 for Arts. 9, 10 and 15. The absolute status still stands on GDPR Art. 22(3) (in force) and the CPPA ADMT rules (effective 1 Jan 2026, compliance 1 Jan 2027).
amendments.proposed: Restate the citation as 'GDPR Art. 22(3); CPPA ADMT regulations; EU AI Act Art. 14(4)–(5) (deferred to 2 Dec 2027 by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)'. Keep absolute on the in-force limbs.
amendments.why_not_applied: A citation that mis-states an instrument's application date is a defect in the rulebook, and the rulebook changes only by enactment (A3, FL-GV-006).

amendments.finding: The provision cites 'EU AI Act Art. 5' as of the original Regulation. Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 inserted a new Art. 5 prohibition on AI systems generating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material, with a transitional period to 2 Dec 2026. The pack's Art. 5 floor therefore has a limb that is enacted but not yet binding, and the provision text ('practices prohibited under Article 5') will silently widen on that date.
amendments.proposed: Add to the citation 'as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 — NCII/CSAM limb binding from 2 Dec 2026', and record in source_status that until then the CSAM limb is carried by the extension's FL-CS-001 under 18 U.S.C. §2252A rather than by Art. 5.
amendments.why_not_applied: Widening an absolute's scope, even by acknowledging an amendment to its source, is a legislative act; the responsible-scaling council should decide whether the limb becomes absolute on 2 Dec 2026 or stays deferred in a separate provision.

amendments.finding: The only absolute in the brand-safety family cites 'risk architecture §5.2' alone. Under Definition 1 an absolute means no one below the legislature may decide, not that the harm is severe. A toxicity threshold is, by the pack's own FL-BS-006 and the 'toxicity_threshold_relaxed_without_approval' factor, a governed parameter with an approval route — which is the signature of an ordinary provision. The provision reads as a severity claim.
amendments.proposed: Either ground the floor in an external instrument (EU AI Act Art. 55(1)(b) systemic-risk mitigation for the flagged-content classes; DSA Art. 16 for illegal content) and narrow it to illegal-content classes, or reclassify it as ordinary with the policy board as the named exception authority.
amendments.why_not_applied: Reclassifying an absolute rewrites which cases short-circuit under A6 and would re-base every F-absolute case that cites it.

amendments.finding: The absolute provenance floor cites 'DSM Directive 2019/790 Art. 4; EDPB Opinion 28/2024'. Verified: Art. 4 of the DSM Directive is the text-and-data-mining exception with its opt-out — it is the source for FL-TD-003, not for a prohibited-provenance bar. The instruments that actually make provenance a floor are EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(e) (untargeted facial-image scraping, in force since 2 Feb 2025) and the EDPB's holding (4) on unlawful development tainting deployment; the LAION appeal (BGH hearing 3 Sept 2026) may also move the Art. 4 contours.
amendments.proposed: Restate the citation as 'EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(e); EDPB Opinion 28/2024 holding (4); DSM Directive 2019/790 Art. 4(3) for the opt-out limb only', and flag the LAION appeal as an instability marker.
amendments.why_not_applied: Changing the grounding of an absolute is a legislative act; the finding is filed for the privacy-and-data-stewardship office.
